description:
XORTil is a technology-driven team interested in using space-based data to solve real-world problems. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are exploring ways to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data to improve fire detection, visualization and analysis.

Our interests include software development, satellite data, artificial intelligence, data analytics and Earth science.

We welcome collaborators with skills in GIS, remote sensing, Python, data science, env science and visualization.
summary:
Harmattan is a web application that merges NASA's two active-fire records, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), into one consistent record and turns it into an interactive burning activity calendar for Nigeria, for the whole country, any of its 37 states, or any area a user draws on the map.

The two sensors cannot be compared directly: VIIRS sees many small fires that MODIS misses, so on held-out years raw VIIRS overstated MODIS-scale burning by 274%. We harmonized them on a common unit (0.1° active-fire cell-days), corrected the early Terra-only years, and calibrated VIIRS to the MODIS scale for each 1° tile. On 2022–2025 data never used for fitting, the bias fell to 3.6% and agreement reached r² = 0.94.

On this 26-year record (6.3 million detections), Harmattan shows when burning normally happens, the critical period for each area (for Nigeria, 14 Dec – 13 Feb, peaking around 11 Jan), how unusual each season was, and whether the last 7 days are below normal, normal, above normal or extreme for the time of year. It gives emergency responders, land managers and scientists a consistent picture of past burning and an early warning for the present, and the method works for any country.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Harmattan answers three questions for any area of Nigeria: When does burning usually happen? Was this season unusual? Is the past week normal or extreme?

• Fire Clock – a spiral with one turn per year, showing every day since November 2000. January is at the top, so the dry-season burning appears as a bright arc that repeats every year, and unusual years stand out at a glance.

• Burning Activity Calendar – a year × day heat grid. A "fire year" mode (July–June) keeps each dry season in one row, because Nigeria's season crosses New Year.

• Seasons and Critical Periods – the normal range for each day of the year (10th–90th percentile and median, 2003–2022) compared with any season. The critical period is detected automatically for each area. For all of Nigeria it runs from 14 Dec to 13 Feb, peaks around 11 Jan and holds 66% of yearly burning, and each state has its own window.

• Anomalies – yearly and monthly z-scores. Example finding: burning in the 2019/20–2024/25 seasons averaged about 27% less than in 2003/04–2007/08, consistent with the decline in African savanna fire reported in the scientific literature.

• Early Warning – the last 7 days of near-real-time detections compared with the same week in 20 baseline years, giving a percentile and a status (Below normal / Normal / Above normal / Extreme), plus the days remaining until the critical period begins.

• Time-lapse Map – more than 300 months of harmonized burning on a NASA Black Marble globe, with the latest detections pulsing on top.

• Harmonization Proof – before/after bias, error and agreement, so users can see why the record can be trusted.

HOW IT WORKS (THE HARMONIZATION)

1. Data: NASA FIRMS yearly archives for Nigeria (MODIS Collection 6.1 for 2000–2025 and VIIRS 375 m Suomi NPP for 2012–2025) plus the 7-day near-real-time feeds, 6.3 million detections in total.

2. Quality filter: MODIS confidence ≥ 30, VIIRS nominal or high, vegetation fires only (this removes gas flares and other static sources).

3. Common unit: each detection is mapped to a 0.1° grid cell and day ("active-fire cell-day"), which removes most of the 1 km vs 375 m pixel-size difference.

4. Terra-only gap: the 2000–2002 period, when only Terra flew, is scaled by monthly Terra+Aqua / Terra ratios fitted on 2003–2011.

5. Calibration: VIIRS is scaled to the MODIS level for each 1° tile, fitted on 2012–2021 and pulled toward the national ratio where data is sparse.

6. Fusion: MODIS and calibrated VIIRS are averaged where both exist; calibrated VIIRS continues the record after MODIS retires.

7. Validation on held-out 2022–2025 data: bias fell from +274% to +3.6%, mean error fell from 109 to 10 cell-days per tile-month, and r² rose from 0.90 to 0.94.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

• Emergency responders get a simple status they can act on, plus advance notice of when the critical period starts.

• Land managers and state agencies can time fire patrols, firebreaks and awareness campaigns to each state's critical window.

• Scientists get a consistent 26-year record that will continue after the MODIS satellites retire.

• The approach uses only free, open NASA data and works for any country FIRMS covers.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The spiral fire clock and the fire-year calendar show the seasonal rhythm of burning in a way a non-specialist understands in seconds. The project is named after the Harmattan, the dry-season wind that coincides with West Africa's burning season.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, Shapely) for the data pipeline; JavaScript with MapLibre GL JS and D3.js for the web app; NASA GIBS map tiles; hosted on GitHub Pages as a fast static site that also works on phones. Source code and method: https://github.com/LanZeroth/XORtil

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Active-fire cell-days measure how often and how widely fires are detected, not burned area. The 2026 yearly archive is not yet published, so January–early November 2026 is shown as "no data". Next steps: calibration by land cover and day/night, adding NOAA-20/21 archives, SMS alerts in local languages, and expanding to all of Africa.
